claim: On the eve of war the Army in India numbered 76,953 British ranks and 239,561 Indian ranks (193,901 Indian combatants: 159,134 serving and 34,767 reservists; 45,660 Indian non-combatants).

evidence.locator: Part XXIX s.7 'India's Military Contribution', book p.777 (pdf p.795), para 1
evidence.quote: At the outbreak of war the strength of the Army in India was: British officers 4,744; British other ranks 72,209; serving 159,134; reservists 34,767; non-combatants, Indian 45,660; grand totals British 76,953, Indian 239,561
At the outbreak of war the strength of the Army in India was: ... Indians serving 159,134; Indian reservists 34,767; Total Indian combatants 193,901; Indian non-combatants 45,660; Grand Total 239,561

notes: S01 and S02 share one origin (India Office / Government of India figures), so this is one owner's count seen twice. The owner is the Government that ran the army, with no reason to understate it. CWGC (S03) gives a looser 'some 150,000 in 1914' (see conflicts K5).

claim: Up to 31 December 1919 India recruited 877,068 combatants and 563,369 non-combatants (Indian ranks): 1,440,437 in all.

evidence.quote: Grand totals recruited in India (Indian ranks) during the war, up to 31st December, 1919. Combatants 877,068; Non-combatants 563,369; Grand total 1,440,437
877,068 combatants and 563,369 non-combatants, making a total of 1,440,437
During the First World War the Indian Army grew from some 150,000 in 1914 to nearly 1.4 million by 1918

notes: S01/S02 share one origin (the India Office); S03 (CWGC) gives 'nearly 1.4 million' without a stated source, so it is not counted as independent: VERIFIED-P. Recruited is not the same as served overseas (C003).

claim: Up to 31 December 1919, 1,096,013 Indians (officers, other ranks and non-combatants) had been sent on service overseas from India; with 285,037 British ranks the total was 1,381,050 all told (which counts 42,430 British ranks sent via England).

evidence.locator: book p.777 (pdf p.795), table 3, bottom line (rendered page image checked)
evidence.quote: Indian 1,096,013; grand total of all ranks 1,338,620; + 42,430 British ranks via the United Kingdom = 1,381,050
and 1,096,013 Indian or to 1,381,050 all told
More than one million service personnel from Indian forces served overseas

notes: 'Over a million' is on S01/S02 (one origin) and in CWGC's 'more than one million' (no stated source, not independent): VERIFIED-P. It counts non-combatants (C004). An earlier GoI figure is 1,302,394 'personnel' despatched from Indian ports up to November 1918 (S02 p.78), which includes British ranks: different scope and date.

claim: Of the 1,096,013 Indians sent overseas, 474,789 (43.3 per cent) were non-combatants, such as labour and followers; 621,224 were Indian combatants (16,162 Indian officers and warrant officers, 605,062 other ranks).

evidence.locator: book p.777 table 3, 'Non-combatants, Indians' column total and combatant columns

method: method/ww1_numbers.py block A: 474,789 / 1,096,013 = 43.3%; 16,162 + 605,062 = 621,224. The theatre totals sum exactly to 1,096,013.
notes: The Indian other-ranks and non-combatant columns sum to within 3 of the printed column totals. The gap is the Aden row, whose parts (480 + 19,936 + 5,786) sum to 26,202 while the row total prints 26,205: a 3-unit inconsistency in the source (or a misread digit in one Aden figure), not OCR of the totals. The printed totals are used. 'Followers' and 'non-combatants' are the source's own words.

claim: By theatre, of 1,096,013 Indians sent overseas: Mesopotamia 675,391 (61.6 per cent), Egypt 143,993, France 138,608 (12.6 per cent), Persian Gulf 49,198, East Africa 47,704, Aden 26,205, Salonica 9,931, Gallipoli 4,950.

evidence.locator: book p.777 table 3, 'Totals: Indian' column (page image checked)
evidence.quote: To France 138,608; To East Africa 47,704; To Mesopotamia 675,391; To Egypt 143,993; To Gallipoli 4,950; To Salonica 9,931; To Palestine 33; To Aden 26,205; To Persian Gulf 49,198

method: method/ww1_numbers.py block A: shares computed against the printed grand total 1,096,013. The nine printed theatre totals sum exactly to it.
notes: Palestine's row reads 4 / 1 / 28 and prints 33 (it reconciles); Aden's parts sum to 26,202 against a printed 26,205 (see C004). The 'France' row here is the Indian share of the 1914-19 total; the infantry left France in late 1915 is NOT yet a verified claim (open question).

claim: SUMMARY: counts of Indian dead differ by whose count it is: 62,056 'lost their lives' (War Office 1922, to 31 Dec 1920); 61,041 'dead from all causes' (Government of India 1923, to 30 Apr 1920 overseas / 19 Sep 1920 frontier); about 74,000 Indian Army dead (CWGC, 4 Aug 1914-31 Aug 1921); and '70,000 servicemen of Undivided India who died between 1914 and 1921' on a second CWGC page; a third CWGC page says 'more than 73,000'. Each separate count is its own claim (C026-C028); this one only records that they differ.

evidence.locator: Part IV s.I Table (i)(a), book p.237 (pdf p.249; page image checked)
evidence.quote: Number of soldiers who lost their lives ... Indian Empire (b) Indian: officers 904; other ranks 61,152; total 62,056 ... wounds 66,889; prisoners 11,070. Footnote: Killed in action; died of wounds; died as prisoners; and missing officers and other ranks whose deaths have been accepted

evidence.locator: Chapter V, p.177 (leaf 184; table on a rotated page, image checked)
evidence.quote: Summary of casualties: Died from all causes 61,041; Wounded 67,771; Missing and prisoners 1,262; Grand total 130,074
approximately 74,000 officers and enlisted men of the Indian Army who died in the First World War

evidence.locator: CWGC 'How to find and visit Indian war dead', Delhi Memorial section
evidence.quote: a national memorial to the 70,000 servicemen of Undivided India who died between 1914 and 1921
First World War: 4 August 1914 to 31 August 1921 (dates inclusive)

evidence.locator: CWGC 'How to find...', 'How many Indian soldiers died in World War 1?'
evidence.quote: We commemorate more than 73,000 Indian servicemen from World War One

method: method/ww1_numbers.py block D. 74,000 - 62,056 = 11,944 and 74,000 - 61,041 = 12,959 (the CWGC window runs 8-14 months later and covers all causes).
notes: Honest wording: 'about sixty to seventy-four thousand, depending on who counts'. Do not say 'over 74,000' as a fact; do not say '62,056' without 'the War Office counted'. GoI's 61,041 includes 18,783 'followers'; the War Office 62,056 is soldiers (officers + other ranks): the bases may differ, which is unresolved (conflicts K1).

claim: In the Government of India's own table of 'dead from all causes', Mesopotamia accounts for 33,462 of 61,041 dead (54.8 per cent) and France for 8,907 (14.6 per cent): about 3.8 Mesopotamia deaths for every one in France.

evidence.locator: Chapter V, p.177 (leaf 184), table 'Dead from all causes' by theatre, rows Mesopotamia and France

method: method/ww1_numbers.py block C: the ten theatre rows sum exactly to each printed grand total; 33,462 / 61,041 = 54.8%; 8,907 / 61,041 = 14.6%.
notes: Single source (Government of India 1923), read from a page image. The table includes British officers and ranks of the Indian Army and 'followers'. Needs the independent checker to re-read the rotated page.

claim: In the Government of India's table, Punjab supplied 349,688 of the 683,149 combatants enlisted in the provinces of British India up to the Armistice (51.2 per cent); the United Provinces 163,578 (23.9 per cent); Bengal 7,117 (about 1 per cent).

evidence.locator: Chapter VII, 'Recruitment by Provinces', printed p.277 (OCR page marker 278 follows the table; djvu line 13739)

method: method/ww1_numbers.py block E: the twelve rows sum exactly to the printed combatant (683,149) and non-combatant (414,493) totals, and each row's total equals its two parts once five typing slips of mine are corrected (Bengal 59,052; NWFP 45,231; Bihar and Orissa 41,552; Central Provinces 15,007; Assam 15,124). The twelve row totals then sum to the printed grand total 1,097,642.
notes: Single owner (GoI). Table is for provinces only: Indian States' 115,891 recruits (same book, p.278) and Nepal's 58,904 are separate. Counting the States' recruits, Punjab is 349,688 of 826,855 combatants = 42.3% (method block E). It is not stated whether 'Punjab' includes the Punjab States. Say 'about half of British India's provincial recruits', not 'half the army'.

claim: In the 1921 Census, the Punjab (with its attached States) had 25.1 million people, about 9 per cent of the 270.9 million in all the provinces: so a place with about a tenth of the people gave about half of the combatant recruits.

evidence.locator: Census of India 1921 Vol I Pt I, Subsidiary Table III, book p.58 (pdf p.78), row 14 Punjab and the 'Provinces' row
evidence.quote: Punjab 25,101,060; Provinces 270,950,433 (read from a low-resolution scan)

method: method/ww1_numbers.py block F: 25,101,060 / 270,950,433 = 9.3%. The 15 province rows sum to 270,932,433, within 18,000 of the printed row, so the digits are consistent. 1921 is after the war: 1911 gives a similar share.
notes: Hedge as 'about a tenth' / 'about half'. A comparison of two different tables from the same Government; the Punjab Census row includes the Punjab States, the recruitment row may not.

claim: The first Indian troops arrived in France at Marseilles on 26 September 1914; the Sirhind Brigade, held back in Egypt, reached Marseilles on 30 November.

evidence.quote: The first convoy arrived on the morning of the 26th September with the Lahore Division and part of the Indian Cavalry Corps
arrived at Marseilles on the 26th September
it finally reached Marseilles on the 30th November

notes: One regimental history written for the Government in 1917. A French defence-archive item and The National Archives' WO 95/3926 were not opened. The first convoy of 26 Sep carried the Lahore Division and part of the Indian Cavalry Corps (not the whole force).

claim: In March 1915 Indian Army forces took part in the attack at Neuve-Chapelle; the CWGC says Indian forces made up around one third of the attacking troops.

evidence.locator: CWGC 'How to find and visit Indian war dead', WW1 war memorials section
evidence.quote: Indian forces accounted for around one third of the attacking troops

notes: CWGC is the owner of the memorial, not of battle statistics, and gives no source for 'one third'. Hedge ('about a third, says the CWGC') or open the Official History.

claim: The Neuve-Chapelle Memorial in France commemorates more than 4,700 Indian soldiers and labourers who died on the Western Front and have no known grave.

evidence.quote: The memorial at Neuve-Chapelle commemorates more than 4,700 Indian soldiers and labourers who died on the Western Front
The Neuve-Chapelle Memorial commemorates over 4,700 Indian soldiers and labourers who lost their lives on the Western Front
commemorates more than 4,700 soldiers and labourers of Undivided India who have no known grave

notes: All three pages are CWGC (one owner, 2018-2025): VERIFIED-P at the owner, not independently corroborated. 'Soldiers and labourers' is the CWGC's wording.

claim: The Delhi Memorial (India Gate) commemorates more than 13,000 servicemen with no known grave or unmaintainable graves, and is also a national memorial to the dead of 'Undivided India' (CWGC: 70,000 who died 1914-1921); it was designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens.

evidence.locator: CWGC 'How to find...', Delhi Memorial (India Gate) section
evidence.quote: the memorial commemorates more than 13,000 Commonwealth servicemen who either have no known grave, or who's graves were unmaintainable

notes: CWGC's own memorial page returned a bot-check (403) and was not read. Inscription as given by CWGC: 'To the dead of the Indian Armies who fell and are honoured in France and Flanders, Mesopotamia and Persia, East Africa, Gallipoli and elsewhere in the near and the Far East and in sacred memory'. Check against the monument itself or the Delhi Memorial page before showing the inscription.

claim: The Mesopotamia Commission (1917) found the Indian Army had been cut back before 1914 on the assumption it would not meet a European power: divisions ready to mobilise were reduced from nine to seven, equipment was set by frontier warfare alone, and medical establishments were the most starved, so it was 'suddenly and unexpectedly called upon' to fight a war for which no preparation had been made.

evidence.locator: Part I, Preface, section C 'Condition of Indian Army on outbreak of war', paras 23-25 (djvu lines 849-890)
evidence.quote: the number of divisions available for immediate mobilisation was reduced from nine to seven
The Indian Army was thus suddenly and unexpectedly called upon to participate largely in an external warfare for which no preparation had been made

notes: A British Parliament commission criticising its own Governments: weak incentive to flatter. It speaks of the Indian Army's equipment and medical care, not of who chose the war. Fresh angle.

claim: The Viceroy, Lord Hardinge, told the Legislative Council on 8 September 1914 that 'five weeks ago ... the British Empire was plunged into war' with Germany and Austria, and read the King-Emperor's message to the 'Princes and Peoples of India'; the Government of India's own book records no vote by Indians on entering the war.

evidence.quote: At the opening of the Legislative Council Session on the 8th September 1914, the Viceroy, Lord Hardinge, made a speech on the war
It is now five weeks ago that the British Empire was plunged into war with the two great military nations, Germany and Austria

notes: The 'no vote' part is an absence in the book, not a statement; keep it out of the script or say only 'the Viceroy told the Council'. Open question: who in law decided India's entry (needs the Government of India Act text or a constitutional record). Do not say 'the Government declared the war for India': C015 supports only what the Viceroy told the Council.

claim: The Government of India's 1923 book says recruitment of Indians 'was effected on a purely voluntary basis', compulsion being applied to European British subjects only.

evidence.locator: Chapter VIII (conclusion), p.294 (OCR page marker 294; djvu line 17610)
evidence.quote: Throughout the war the recruitment of Indians was effected on a purely voluntary basis, the principle of compulsion being applied to European British subjects only

notes: This is the Government's claim about itself (an interested party). No independent record of how recruiting was done (pressure on villages, quotas) was opened: see open_questions. Never state 'voluntary' as our own fact.

claim: Recruits to combatant ranks were temporarily offered a bonus of Rs. 50, plus Rs. 15 more on finishing training or going overseas; troops serving in Europe and the Eastern theatres received a 25 per cent field allowance.

evidence.locator: Chapter VI 'Pay and allowances', pp.242-243 (djvu lines 10405-10425)
evidence.quote: A bonus of Rs. 50 to combatant recruits was temporarily offered. In addition recruits received a farther Rs. 15 on completing their training, or on proceeding overseas
received a 25 per cent. increase on pay as special field allowance

notes: Pay and bonus are what the Government offered; no document opened says they were why men enlisted.

claim: At the Delhi War Conference of April 1918 India undertook to find half a million recruits in the twelve months from 1 June 1918, although only 270,000 combatant recruits had been obtained in the previous year; about 200,000 were enrolled by the Armistice.

evidence.quote: India undertook to contribute half a million recruits during the twelve months commencing on 1st June 1918, although during the previous year only 270,000 combatant recruits had been obtained. By the date of the Armistice (11th November 1918) some 200,000 had been enrolled

notes: Gandhi's own part in this conference (CWMG vol. 14) was not read at source: see open_questions.

claim: In 1917 the Government of India, with the 'general assent' of the Imperial Legislative Council, offered Britain a lump sum of GBP 100 million for the war; nearly GBP 75 million was raised by war loans in India; the Government says this added over 30 per cent to India's national debt and was more than a year's income.

evidence.quote: offer His Majesty's Government a lump sum of £100 millions as a special contribution by India towards the expenses of the war
nearly £75 millions were raised in India by the war loans of 1917 and 1918
it adds over 30 per cent. to India's national debt

notes: The Government's own account; the 'income' comparison is its claim. Not independently checked.

claim: On 20 August 1917, in mid-war, the British Government declared its policy to be 'the increasing association of Indians in every branch of the administration and the gradual development of self-governing institutions with a view to the progressive realisation of responsible Government in India as an integral part of the British Empire'.

evidence.locator: Hansard, Commons, 6 Aug 1918, Mr. Montagu's statement (Montagu reads his announcement of 20 Aug 1917)
evidence.quote: the increasing association of Indians in every branch of the administration and the gradual development of self-governing institutions with a view to the progressive realisation of responsible Government in India as an integral part of the British Empire

notes: Verbatim words are the Government's. The 20 August 1917 date is from Montagu's own sentence in the 1918 speech ('on the 20th of August last year'). It is not claimed that Indians fought for this; the record gives no such link.

claim: Indian soldiers' own words, as translated and passed by the British censor, show mixed feelings: 'Fighting is our duty and to die on the field of battle is an excellent thing' (Gulab Ram, 6th Jats, Sept 1915); 'I do not al all like this, but I am helpless ... my family will get an allowance ... Now I am alone' (Duli Chand, July 1915, transcribed as written).

evidence.locator: IOR/L/MIL/5/825/6 f.24r (Gulab Ram, 6th Jats, to Sej Ram, Rohtak; Hindi, Sep 1915), via the New Forest transcription
evidence.quote: Fighting is our duty and to die on the field of battle is an excellent thing. Such an opportunity will not occur again, and it is a question of luck.

evidence.locator: IOR/L/MIL/5/825/4 f.136 (Duli Chand, Barton on Sea; Hindi, July 1915)
evidence.quote: I do not al all like this, but I am helpless. The battle is very severe and now but such is my fate that a bullet has not killed me. However, fate is not to be relied on, and you ought to know that my family will get an allowance.

notes: Two letters among thousands the censor chose to extract, translated by British staff, typed by volunteers. Duli Chand does not give the allowance as his reason for fighting: he says he dislikes going back and is helpless. Do not use 'family allowance' as a motive. The original British Library pages were not opened. Say 'one soldier wrote', never 'soldiers said'.

claim: The CWGC counts First World War dead for the period 4 August 1914 to 31 August 1921 (dates inclusive).

evidence.locator: CWGC policy, Eligibility criteria, 'First World War' dates
evidence.quote: First World War: 4 August 1914 to 31 August 1921 (dates inclusive)

notes: This is why the CWGC total can exceed the War Office total (C006).

claim: The war's casualties among Indians, in the War Office table, also included 66,889 wounded and 11,070 'reported prisoners of war'.

evidence.quote: wounds received: other ranks 65,209, total 66,889; prisoners of war: total 11,070

notes: Government of India's own table (C006 S02) gives 67,771 wounded and 1,262 'missing and prisoners' (a different definition: 'prisoners repatriated are not shown'). Use neither without the owner's name.

claim: The CWGC describes the Indian memorials and its Indian totals as those of 'Undivided India' (the India of 1914-21, before partition); the Government of India's province table for the war names Punjab, Bengal, the North-West Frontier Province and Baluchistan among the recruiting provinces.

evidence.quote: commemorates more than 4,700 soldiers and labourers of Undivided India who have no known grave

evidence.locator: Chapter VII, p.277-278 'Recruitment by Provinces' (djvu line 13739)
evidence.quote: Province. Combatant recruits enlisted ... Punjab ... North-West Frontier Province ... Baluchistan ... Bengal

notes: Wording point. The Government's book also counts 58,904 recruits from Nepal separately (p.278). Which of today's countries each province lies in is a modern-map fact to take from the house geodata, not from these documents.

claim: The War Office's 1922 table counts 62,056 Indian soldiers (904 officers, 61,152 other ranks) who 'lost their lives' in the Great War to 31 December 1920 (killed in action, died of wounds, died as prisoners, and missing accepted as dead).

evidence.locator: Part IV s.I Table (i)(a), book p.237 (pdf p.249; page image checked), row 'Indian Empire (b) Indian'
evidence.quote: lost their lives: officers 904, other ranks 61,152, total 62,056; footnote: Killed in action; died of wounds; died as prisoners; and missing officers and other ranks whose deaths have been accepted for official purposes

notes: The table's own note says the casualty figures were prepared during the war and were subject to correction; the final ones are in Cmd. 1193 (General Annual Report of the British Army 1913-1919), not opened. Whether disease deaths are included is not stated in the footnote.

claim: The Government of India's 1923 book counts 61,041 Indian Army dead 'from all causes' up to 30 April 1920 for overseas forces and 19 September 1920 for frontier operations (1,467 British officers, 847 Indian officers, 1,195 British ranks, 38,749 Indian ranks, 18,783 followers).

evidence.locator: Chapter V, p.177 (leaf 184; rotated table, image checked), 'Grand totals' row and 'Summary of casualties'
evidence.quote: Dead from all causes 61,041; grand totals 1,467 | 847 | 1,195 | 38,749 | 18,783

notes: The count includes British officers and ranks of the Indian Army and followers, and the frontier operations (4,968 deaths, which are not overseas).

claim: The CWGC counts about 74,000 Indian Army dead of the First World War (period 4 August 1914 to 31 August 1921), of which about 8,000 are in CWGC war cemeteries and about 65,000 commemorated by name on a memorial; its older page says 74,000 of 160,950 Indian-force dead in both world wars.

evidence.quote: approximately 74,000 officers and enlisted men of the Indian Army who died in the First World War
74,000 of the First World War and 87,000 of the Second World War

notes: One owner (CWGC), pages dated 2018 and 2025. The 8,000 + 65,000 = 73,000 split on S04, 'more than 73,000' on S05 and '70,000' on another page differ from 'approximately 74,000' (K2).
